title: A Bike Park Behind the Teaching Building
paragraphs: On the first Monday of September, a middle school in Baiyun opened a small bike park behind the teaching building. It has room for sixty bikes and two air pumps. Before this year, students left their bikes along the school wall, and on windy days some of them fell over like dominoes.

The park took four months to plan. The school asked students what they needed, and more than three hundred wrote the same answer: a place where bikes do not fall. A group of eight students then measured the space and drew a plan on paper. Their first plan had room for only forty bikes, so they turned the racks sideways and found twenty more places.

Grade 8 student Lin, who led the group, said the hardest part was not the drawing. It was the rain. The ground used to hold water after a storm, and bikes stood in it for hours. The new park has a small drain in the middle and a roof made of light metal sheets.

The school spent about nine thousand yuan on the park. A teacher said the money came from a fund for small repairs, and the bike park was chosen because it helped the most students. Now about fifty students use it every day.

There is still one problem. Some students park their bikes in a hurry and block the gate. Lin's group put a sign on the wall: park straight, leave in a line. It works most days. On Friday, when everyone wants to go home at the same time, it does not.

title: The Library That Opens at Seven
paragraphs: Every morning at seven, a small library on the third floor of a middle school in Tianhe opens its door. Only five or six students are waiting, but the librarian, Ms Zhou, says the early hour is the most important hour of her day.

The library used to open at eight. Last year a student wrote a note and put it in the suggestion box: I get to school at half past six because my parents go to work early, and I have nowhere to sit. Ms Zhou read the note three times and then asked the school if she could start work an hour earlier.

The school said yes, but there was a catch. Someone had to be on duty, and the library had only two staff members. Ms Zhou now opens the door at seven and leaves at four. Her colleague starts later and stays until six.

The early students are quiet. Most of them read, some do homework, and a few just sleep with their heads on their arms. Ms Zhou does not wake them. She says a warm room with a chair is sometimes all a student needs before a long day.

In the first month, nineteen different students came before eight o'clock. By November the number was forty-one. Ms Zhou keeps a small notebook and writes down one thing each morning: who came, what they read, how long they stayed. She says the notebook is not for the school. It is for her, to remember why she gets up so early.

title: Ten Minutes of Running Before Class
paragraphs: At half past seven, a middle school in Haizhu plays a short piece of music over the loudspeakers. Students put down their books and walk to the track. For ten minutes, they run, walk, or jog in a slow circle. Then they go back to class.

The idea came from a physical education teacher, Mr Huang. He noticed that students in the first class of the morning were sleepy. Some could not answer a simple question until the second class. He asked the school for ten minutes and got five, and then asked again and got ten.

Not everyone liked it at first. Some students said running made them tired, not awake. Others said ten minutes was too short to be useful. Mr Huang asked them to try for three weeks and write down how they felt.

The results were mixed. About half of the students said they felt more awake. A smaller group said they felt the same. Only seven students said they felt worse. Mr Huang said the mixed result was honest and useful, and he did not expect everyone to agree.

Now the school runs the ten minutes four days a week. On the fifth day, students can choose to walk instead. One grade 7 student said she likes the walking day best, because she can talk with her friends before the bell. Mr Huang says that is fine too. The point is to move a little, not to run fast.

title: A Lunch Menu Written by Students
paragraphs: For two weeks in October, students at a middle school in Yuexiu chose their own lunch. A group of twelve students worked with the kitchen to plan ten meals, and every day the school sold what the group had chosen.

The plan started with a survey. The group asked four hundred students one question: which dish do you always finish? Rice with tomato and egg came first. Fried chicken came second. Green vegetables came last, with only thirty votes.

The group did not simply follow the votes. They asked the kitchen what was cheap, what was easy to cook for six hundred people, and what could be kept warm for an hour. Three of the top five dishes failed these tests. Fried chicken was too slow to cook in large amounts, and one soup lost its taste when it stood too long.

In the end, the menu had rice, noodles, two kinds of vegetables, and one meat dish each day. The green vegetables stayed, but the group asked the kitchen to cook them in a different way: less water, more garlic, and a shorter time in the pot.

The result was better than the group expected. On average, students left about a third less food on their plates than in September. A grade 8 student in the group said the biggest lesson was simple: people eat more of what they choose, but they still need someone to choose well.

title: The Boy Who Fixed Thirty Chairs
paragraphs: In a storage room behind the workshop of a middle school in Liwan, thirty chairs are stacked in a corner. Each one has a new screw, a new rubber foot, or a new piece of wood. They were repaired by one student, a grade 8 boy named Chen, over four months.
It started by accident. Chen's own chair had a loose leg, and the workshop teacher said he could fix it himself if he wanted. It took him forty minutes and two attempts. The second attempt worked.

After that he began to notice broken chairs everywhere. Some wobbled, some had sharp edges, and some had lost their rubber feet and made a loud noise on the floor. He asked the school if he could take them to the workshop and bring them back the next day.

The school agreed but asked him to keep a record. Chen wrote down the date, the problem, and what he did. The record shows that most chairs had only one small problem, and that a screw and five minutes were often enough.

Chen says he is not good at many things, but he is patient. He also says the work taught him something about school: hundreds of small things break every year, and nobody notices until someone decides to fix them. The school now keeps a box of screws and rubber feet in the workshop, and three other students have joined him on Wednesday afternoons.

title: One Question a Day
paragraphs: Every morning, a grade 7 class in Panyu writes one question on the board. The question is not from the textbook. It comes from a student, and it must be something the class cannot answer in one sentence.

The idea belongs to the class teacher, Ms Li. She said students asked her many questions, but usually about homework and tests. She wanted them to ask about other things: why the school gate faces east, why the bell sounds different at noon, why the classroom is cold in the morning and warm in the afternoon.

The rule is simple. Anyone can write a question on a small card and put it in a box. Each morning, one card is drawn and copied onto the board. During the last five minutes of the day, the class talks about it. Nobody has to know the answer.

Some questions were solved in a week. One was about the school gate: it faces east because the road was built that way in 1998, before the school moved here. Others are still open. A student asked why the same amount of homework feels different on different days, and the class has argued about it for a month.

Ms Li says the five minutes are the quietest part of her day. She also says the box has changed how students talk. They now ask before they decide something is boring. In November, the class had sixty-four cards in the box, and only nine were about tests.

title: The Noise on the Fourth Floor
paragraphs: For three weeks, students on the fourth floor of a middle school in Tianhe complained about a strange noise. It came every afternoon at about two o'clock, a low knock that seemed to come from inside the wall.

The school first thought it was a water pipe. A worker opened a small panel and found nothing wrong. Then someone suggested it might be a bird. Two students were asked to stand in the corridor for a week and listen.
On the fourth day, they found it. A pigeon had got into the space between the wall and the ceiling and was moving along a metal bar. The knock was the sound of its feet, carried through the wall.

Getting the bird out took two hours. The worker made a small opening near a window, put a plate of rice inside, and waited. The pigeon came out at about five o'clock, walked along the windowsill, and flew away.

The whole thing was small, but it changed one thing at school. The two students who listened for a week now keep a notebook of sounds in the building: the bell, the lift, the rain on the metal roof, a door that closes too hard. Their teacher says they are learning to listen, which is harder than it sounds. In December they played five of the sounds to the class and asked everyone to guess what made them. Only two people guessed the lift, and nobody guessed the door.

title: A Test With No Time Limit
paragraphs: In November, a grade 8 maths class in Huangpu took a test with no time limit. Students could take ten minutes or two hours. The only rule was that they could not take the paper home.

The teacher, Mr Wu, said he got the idea from a student's question. After a normal test, a boy asked him: if I know how to do the last question but I am slow, is my answer worth less? Mr Wu did not have a good answer.
The test had eight questions. Four were easy, two were medium, and two were hard. Students wrote the time they finished on the top of the paper, and Mr Wu did not mark it down.

The results surprised him. Almost everyone finished the easy questions in twenty minutes. Then the class split: about half stopped and handed in the paper, and the other half stayed for more than an hour, working on the two hard questions.

What interested Mr Wu most was what happened to the students who stayed. Many of them did not solve the hard questions, but their writing showed more steps and fewer crossed-out lines. He said the test did not measure who was fast. It measured who was willing to keep thinking after the easy part was done. Next term he plans to use the same test with one change: students must write down how long they thought about each question.

title: The Class That Planted a Garden
paragraphs: Behind a middle school in Zengcheng, a piece of land about the size of two classrooms now holds radishes, lettuce, and a row of small sunflowers. It was a quiet corner with hard soil and old bricks until a grade 7 class asked if they could use it.

The class teacher, Mr Deng, said yes on one condition: the students had to do everything themselves. That meant clearing the bricks, turning the soil, and finding seeds. The school gave them tools and a tap, and nothing else.

The first month was a failure. They planted too early, the seeds did not come up, and the soil was too hard for roots to grow. A student's grandfather, who farms near the school, came to look and told them one thing: the soil needs air, not water.

They turned the soil again, mixed in dry leaves, and waited two weeks before planting. This time the radishes came up in six days. The class now has a watering plan on the wall, with names next to each day of the week.

In December they harvested about twelve kilograms of vegetables and gave them to the school kitchen. It was not enough for one meal. Mr Deng said that was not the point. The point was that the class now knows how long a radish takes to grow, and that a plan on paper is only a plan until the soil says otherwise.

title: Fifteen Minutes Without a Phone
paragraphs: At a middle school in Baiyun, students now leave their phones in a box at the start of the morning break. They get them back fifteen minutes later. The rule started in September and covers all grade 7 and grade 8 classes.

The school did not ban phones. Students still use them after school and during lunch. The fifteen minutes are a small test: what happens when nobody can look at a screen during the break between the second and third classes.

At first, many students just stood around. A teacher said the corridor was strangely quiet for a week. Then things began to change. Someone brought a rope and started skipping. A group began playing a card game with pictures of animals. Two boys started a chess game that lasted four days.

Not everyone is happy. Some students say the rule is unfair, because they use the break to message their parents. The school answered by putting two public phones near the office, and by letting students who need to call home ask a teacher at any time.

A survey in November asked students one question: is the break better or worse than before? About sixty percent said better, twenty percent said the same, and twenty percent said worse. The school says it will keep the rule for one year and then ask again. A grade 8 student wrote on the survey: I still want my phone, but I like the chess game more.

title: The Table Under the Window
paragraphs: On a rainy Saturday in March, four people in Haizhu carried an old wooden table down four floors and into a small truck. The table had been in the family for forty years. It was moving to a new flat two streets away, and the family had already argued about it twice.

The new flat is smaller. The table is 160 centimeters long, and the new dining room is only 190 centimeters wide. The mother wanted to buy a new one for about 1,200 yuan. The father said no. His mother had bought the table in 1986 for sixty yuan, and he did his homework on it.

In the end they called a carpenter, Mr Luo, who lives in the same building. He looked at the table for ten minutes and gave them two choices. He could cut twenty centimeters off each end for 300 yuan, or he could fix the loose leg and leave the size alone for 120 yuan.

They chose the second. Mr Luo tightened three screws, added a small piece of wood under one corner, and rubbed oil into the top. The work took two hours. "A new table is flat and quiet," he said. "This one talks when you put a cup down. Some people like that."

The table now stands under the window, and five can sit around it. There is a dark mark near one end where a hot pot burned the wood in 1998. Nobody has tried to remove it. The mother says she is still thinking about a new table, but she has not looked at prices since.

title: Forty-Six Recipes in Two Handwritings
paragraphs: For six months, a grade 8 student in Liwan copied her grandmother's recipe notebook into a computer. The notebook has forty-six recipes in blue ink, on paper that is turning yellow. Last month she printed four copies and gave them to her mother, two aunts, and her grandmother.

The hard part was not the typing. It was the amounts. The student and her mother cooked twenty-two of the dishes on weekends to test them. They weighed everything and wrote down the times. The sweet and sour pork took four tries before the family agreed it tasted like the old one.

The project cost about 260 yuan, mostly for printing and a hard cover. Her aunt asked why she did not simply photograph the pages. "My grandmother does not write down times," the student said. "She writes down feelings. I had to turn feelings into numbers, so a photo would not work."

The printed book has forty-six recipes, a photo of the old notebook on the first page, and three empty pages at the back. The grandmother has already written two new dishes on them, in the same blue ink. The student says she will need a second printing before the end of the year.

title: Six Tomato Plants on a Small Balcony
paragraphs: In April, a father and his daughter in Liwan began a small garden on their balcony. The balcony is three meters long and one meter wide. They put six tomato plants in old rice bags, because pots were too expensive and the bags were free from a shop downstairs.

The first month did not go well. They watered the plants every morning, and the soil stayed wet all day. Two plants turned yellow and died. The daughter, who is in grade 7, looked in a book and found that tomato roots need air, not only water.

They changed the plan. They made holes in the bottom of each bag, mixed in dry leaves, and watered only when the top of the soil felt dry. They also moved the bags to the sunny end of the balcony, so the plants got light before eleven in the morning.

The cost was small: 40 yuan for soil, 12 yuan for seeds, and nothing for bags. "I thought we would save money," the father said. "We did not. A bag of tomatoes in the market costs less. But my daughter now knows where a tomato comes from, and she looks at the leaves every morning."

By August they had picked forty-one tomatoes. They were smaller than the ones in the market, and one had a deep cut from a fall. The family ate them with eggs and gave eight to a neighbour. Next spring the daughter wants to try beans, and her father has already saved four bags.

title: One Alarm Clock, Two Brothers
paragraphs: Two brothers in Tianhe share a room that is nine square meters. For years they used one alarm clock, and for years it caused trouble. The older boy, 15, leaves at 6:40 for swimming practice. The younger one, 12, does not need to get up until 7:10.

The clock sat between their beds and rang at 6:05. The older brother got up. The younger one pulled the blanket over his head and could not sleep again. In September their mother counted the mornings: in twenty school days, the younger boy was late three times and fell asleep in class twice.

Their father bought a second clock for 45 yuan. It broke in two weeks. Then the family tried something cheaper. They put a small chart on the door with two columns and a pen. Whoever got up first wrote the time. Whoever stayed in bed drew a line.

The chart did not solve the noise, but it changed the argument. The younger brother began to get up at 6:30 on purpose, drink water, and read for twenty minutes. "I stopped fighting the clock," he said. "I started using it. The morning is quiet, and nobody wants the bathroom then."

The chart has been on the door for four months. It shows that the younger boy got up before 6:40 on sixty-one of eighty school days. The older brother says the room is still too small. Their mother says the room did not change. The two of them did.

title: The Photo Behind the Stairs
paragraphs: In January, workers repairing the stairs of an old house in Yuexiu found a photo between two boards. The photo was small, black and white, and bent at one corner. On the back someone had written a date: 12 May 1996.

The house belongs to the Huang family. Three generations have lived there. The photo shows four young people in front of a wall, and a dog at the left. Nobody could name all four. The grandmother, who is 81, looked at it for a long time, then pointed at the second person from the right.

It was her sister, who moved to a town near Zengcheng in 1999 and died in 2014. The family had lost touch with her children. The grandmother had one old phone number, written in a small book, and it no longer worked.

Her granddaughter, a grade 8 student, spent three weekends searching. She found a cousin through a local group for people from that town. The cousin sent a photo of the same wall, taken last year. The wall is still there, but the tree in front of it is gone.

In April, seven people from two branches of the family met for lunch. They brought the photo and put it on the table. The grandmother cried once and then talked for two hours. The photo now hangs in the front room, in a 60 yuan frame. The granddaughter says the frame is the cheapest part.

title: Dinner at Ten Past Nine
paragraphs: For eleven years, the Huang family in Baiyun ate dinner at seven. Since March, they eat at ten past nine. The change came from the father's new job in a restaurant kitchen, where he works from eleven in the morning until half past nine at night.

The first week was hard. The daughter, 13, came home from school at five and was hungry by six. She ate bread and then did not want rice at nine. Her mother ate alone at seven and then sat with them without eating. Nobody liked the new table time.

They tried three plans. The first was for the daughter to eat at six and sit with her father later. That lasted four days. The second was for the mother to cook twice, which she refused after one week. The third plan was a warm box with a thick lid.

Now the mother cooks at six and puts the father's food in the box. The daughter eats a small bowl at six and at nine. "I do not care about food," the father said. "I care that there are three chairs. If I eat alone at ten, I am just a man in a kitchen."

They keep a record on the fridge. Since March they have eaten together eighty-eight of one hundred and twelve nights. On the other nights, the father came home after ten because of a late group. The daughter says she likes nine o'clock, because she finishes her homework and then has something to look forward to.

title: The Dog That Walked Home
paragraphs: On the evening of 6 October, a family in Panyu lost their dog. Doubao, a small brown dog, ran out when the gate stood open for two minutes. The family looked for him until midnight, walking along the river and calling his name, and found nothing.

The next morning they made three hundred flyers and put them on walls near the market, the school, and the bus stop. Printing cost 90 yuan. The daughter, 12, wrote the phone number on the last forty by hand, because the shop had run out of paper.

Nine days passed. The family put a bowl of water and an old shirt near the gate, because a neighbour said dogs follow smell. On the tenth day, a security guard called. He had seen a small brown dog sleeping under a bridge, four kilometers from the house.

The guard, Mr Feng, said the dog was thin but walked to him when he called. "He looked at me like I was late," Mr Feng said. "I did not know his name, so I said hey, and he came anyway." The family offered him 500 yuan. He refused and asked for a photo instead.

Doubao had lost about 1.5 kilograms and had a cut foot. The vet bill was 260 yuan. The family now keeps the gate closed with a hook that cost 8 yuan. The girl still checks the hook twice before bed, and Doubao now sleeps inside, on the old shirt that smells of the gate.

title: Moving Into a Smaller Flat
paragraphs: In July, a family of four in Haizhu moved from a flat of ninety square meters to one of sixty-two. The new flat is on the sixth floor and has two small bedrooms instead of three. The move took three days, and eleven boxes were still unpacked in September.

The hard part was not carrying furniture. It was deciding what to keep. The mother made a rule: if nobody had used something for two years, it would leave. In the end the family gave away forty boxes of things: clothes, toys, pans, and a broken fan that had stood in the corner since 2016.

One argument lasted a week. The daughter, 14, wanted to keep the piano. The flat has no wall for it, and the piano is 150 centimeters wide. The mother said it could go to the school. The daughter said a school piano is not the same. In the end they sold it for 3,000 yuan.

"I thought I would feel lighter," the mother said. "I felt tired for a month instead." The family kept a list of everything they gave away, partly to remember it and partly because the father wanted to know if they would miss it. The list has ninety-four lines.

By October, the flat felt normal. The daughter practises on a keyboard that fits under her bed, for 400 yuan. The family eats two steps from the kitchen. The father says he walks less and talks more. The eleven unpacked boxes are still in the corner, and nobody has opened them.

title: The Water Bill on the Fridge
paragraphs: In May, a family in Tianhe got a water bill for thirty-eight tons. The month before, they had used eighteen. The mother put the bill on the fridge with a magnet and said nobody could take it down until they found the reason.

They checked the usual things first. The washing machine ran four times a week, the same as before. Nobody had filled the small pool on the balcony. The father read the meter twice a day for three days and wrote the numbers on the back of the bill.

The numbers showed a strange thing. Between two in the morning and five, when everyone was asleep, the meter still moved. The daughter, 13, heard water running in the toilet one night and told her father. The rubber part inside the tank had worn out, and water was going down the pipe all night.

A plumber came on a Saturday and changed the part in twenty minutes. He charged 120 yuan, including the visit. "People look at the big things," he said. "A tap that drips is easy to hear. A toilet that runs quietly is not. You notice it only at night, and only if you listen."

The next bill was seventeen tons, one less than before. The family now reads the meter on the first of every month and writes it on a card. The daughter says the card was her idea. Her father says it was his. The bill is still on the fridge, with two numbers on the back.

title: Eight Minutes Every Sunday
paragraphs: Since February, a family in Zengcheng has held a video call every Sunday at seven in the evening. The call is between a grandfather who lives alone and his son's family, who live forty minutes away by car. Most calls last about eight minutes.

The idea came from the granddaughter, who is 12. Before the calls, the family visited the grandfather once a month, and the phone was used only for short messages about weather and food. She said her grandfather did not know what to say on the phone, so he usually said nothing at all.

The first calls were slow. The grandfather held the phone too close, so only his ear and the ceiling could be seen. He asked the same three questions each time: have you eaten, is it cold, and how is school. The granddaughter wrote five new questions on a card and put it by his chair.

The family bought him a simple phone for 700 yuan with a bigger screen. The network in his building is weak, so the picture often stops for two or three seconds. "I do not need to see the whole face," he said. "I need to hear the voice and know they are in the room."

By November they had made forty-one calls, and only three were missed. The grandfather now keeps the card in his shirt pocket. The granddaughter says the best call was in October, when he showed her a bird on his windowsill and forgot to ask any of his three questions.

title: The Rain Gauge That Ran Over
paragraphs: On the afternoon of 12 June, a rain gauge at a middle school in Baiyun ran over for the first time in six years. The gauge holds thirty centimeters of water and stands in an open corner of the playground. When the weather club checked it at noon, it held only two.

The rain began at half past two and stopped at four. Eight students took turns to empty the gauge into a bucket and write down each number. They emptied it three times, and the three readings came to twenty-one centimeters. Water crossed the school road and stood three centimeters deep at the music room door.

"We have seen heavy rain before," said Mr Liang, the geography teacher who runs the club. "But this rain was faster than our hands. For twenty minutes we did nothing but carry buckets from the gauge to the drain."

The old gauge cost about 200 yuan and was bought in 2019. Its glass has a small crack near the top, and the club has covered the crack with tape twice. A new gauge costs 460 yuan, but the money was not approved until July.

Until it arrives, the club writes the morning reading on a board in the corridor. On 13 June the board showed twenty-one centimeters, the highest mark since the school opened. Three students took photos of it before the water on the road had dried.

title: A Night of Frost in the Vegetable Fields
paragraphs: On the night of 18 December, the temperature in a village in Conghua fell to two degrees below zero. It was the earliest frost in eleven years. Farmers in the valley had one night to save their winter vegetables.

Mr Pan, who grows vegetables on thirty mu of land, called his neighbours at nine. By ten, forty people were in the fields with headlights, straw, and long rolls of plastic. They worked until three in the morning, covering row after row and pressing the edges down with stones.

They saved twenty-two of the thirty mu. The plastic cost 1,800 yuan, and the straw came from a shed where it had stood for two years. At four in the morning the temperature fell again, to three degrees below zero.
"We did not save everything," Mr Pan said. "The low field near the stream lost half. Cold air runs down there at night and sits like water in a bowl. Next year I will move the seedlings up the hill."

A neighbour, Mr Deng, said covering the fields early keeps the soil too warm and makes plants weak. The two men argued for ten minutes in the dark. In the morning, the covered rows had lost about ten percent, and the open rows had lost more than half.
The vegetables went to market on 20 December and sold for 1.4 times the usual price. Mr Pan has ordered two hundred more meters of plastic, and he now keeps a thermometer on the wall of his shed.

title: Forty-One Days Above Thirty-Five
paragraphs: Between 1 July and 10 August, a weather station near a middle school in Panyu recorded forty-one days above thirty-five degrees. The hottest day was 23 July, at 39.4 degrees. The school had never moved its timetable for heat before.

This year it did. Physical education moved to before eight in the morning or after five in the afternoon. The school put six water stations in the corridors and gave out about two hundred cups a day. Shade nets went over two courts, at a cost of 12,000 yuan.

The nets did not last. Nine days after they went up, a storm pulled one down and tore a corner. The court stayed closed for four days while workers tied it again with stronger rope. Students played cards in the shade of the stairs instead.

"In June we played basketball at two in the afternoon," said Huang, a grade 8 student. "Nobody wanted to. The ball was too hot to hold, and we drank water until we felt sick. Now we play at seven, and the court is full."

The electricity bill rose by 2,300 yuan in July, mostly for fans and two old air conditioners. The grade 9 building cannot take more machines, because its wires were laid in 2004 and the office says they are already near their limit.
On 11 August, the first rain in six weeks fell. Students stood at the windows and counted the minutes out loud. It lasted eleven. The shade nets stayed up, and the water stations stayed open.

title: Three Days Without Power After the Typhoon
paragraphs: The typhoon arrived on the night of 2 September, with wind near 130 kilometers an hour. At 11:40, power went out in a village in Zengcheng. Two hundred and sixty homes went dark at the same moment, and the rain kept falling until morning.

The first morning showed the damage. Three trees had fallen across the only road into the village, and seventeen poles were down along the fields. Workers cut the trees with saws and pulled the wires out of the mud. It took a full day to open the road.

Power came back in stages. Sixty homes had it on the second evening, and the rest on the third afternoon, after seventy-two hours. A shop owner, Ms He, lost the food in her freezer: about 120 kilograms of fish and meat, worth 6,000 yuan.

"I bought four hundred yuan of ice on the first day," she said. "It kept the fish cold for one night, and then it was water. Nobody thinks about a freezer until it stops, and then it is the only thing you think about."

Repairs to her shop cost another 900 yuan. She has no insurance for food and did not ask the village for help. In October she bought a small generator for 2,300 yuan, and she now keeps two bags of ice beside it.

The village has asked the power company to cut the branches near the line before next summer. The company said it would send a team in March. Ms He has written that date on the wall behind her counter.

title: The Morning the Ferry Waited
paragraphs: At six on the morning of 5 March, fog covered the river near a town in Panyu. A worker at the dock could not see the other bank, ninety meters away. The first boat of the day did not leave at 6:20 as usual.

The captain, Mr Feng, waited two hours and ten minutes. One hundred and forty passengers stood on the dock or sat on the low wall. Every two minutes the ferry sounded its horn, so that other boats would know where it was.

Among the passengers was a woman holding a box with a cake inside. She was going to a shop opening in the next town and had paid 180 yuan for the cake. She put the box on her knees and did not open it once.

"I have waited in fog before," Mr Feng said. "Once for four hours. The river is wide and the current is strong, and a boat that leaves too early is not brave, it is stupid. Passengers are angry for ten minutes, and then they understand."

The company lost about 2,000 yuan in fares that morning, and three boats stayed at the dock. The fog lifted at half past eight, and the ferry arrived at 8:52. The cake was still cold when the woman reached the shop.

Since April, the dock has printed a fog timetable on yellow paper and given copies to the three boat crews. It says one thing in large letters: the boat leaves when the captain can see the other bank.

title: When the Walls Stayed Wet
paragraphs: For nine days in March, the walls and floors of a middle school in Liwan stayed wet. Water ran down the inside of the windows, and the air felt like a warm, wet towel. It happens every spring, but this year it lasted longer than anyone could remember.

Six caretakers worked on the corridors, about two hundred meters in total. They put down towels three times a day and set out nine yellow signs. Even so, nine students slipped in the first week, and one cut his hand on a door.

The first fix made things worse. A teacher opened all the windows to let in dry air, and the walls turned wetter within an hour. A science teacher explained why: water in the air turns into drops when it touches something cold, and the outside air was warmer than the walls.

"People think we are not cleaning," said Ms Zhou, who has worked at the school for twelve years. "The floor is clean. It is the sky that is on it. I tell students to walk as if they are on ice, and they laugh, and then they slip."

The school bought two dehumidifiers for 1,600 yuan each. Thirty classrooms share them, so each machine runs for about two hours a day. On the twelfth day a north wind came through the city, and the floors were dry in four hours.
The yellow signs stayed in a cupboard for the rest of the term. Ms Zhou says she will take them out again next March, on the very first wet morning the windows run with water.

title: Cutting Three Hundred Trees Before the Wind
paragraphs: From 10 to 24 May, a team of fourteen workers cut branches from 312 trees along a road in Tianhe. The work started at seven each morning and ended at five. Two lifts moved slowly along the road, and trucks carried away sixty loads of branches.

The city does this every year before the rainy season. A tree with too many branches catches the wind like a sail. Workers cut about thirty percent of each crown, keeping the shape and leaving the main limbs.

Not everyone agreed. Ms Liang, 63, has lived on the road for thirty years and has watched one banyan since it was small. She stood under it on 12 May and asked the workers to stop. She said the tree looked naked and would not survive the summer.

"I understand her," said one worker, Mr Luo. "But a branch that breaks in a storm is heavier than a car. Two years ago a limb fell on a bus stop at night. Nobody was there, and that was luck, not planning."

The season gave a mixed answer. In July, three trees on the road still fell, including one that hit a parked car and cost 4,000 yuan to repair. No one was hurt. The banyan that Ms Liang protected lost one branch and kept its shape.
In October the city planted forty young trees along the same road, in places where old ones had stood. Ms Liang wrote to the office and asked for one outside her building. She got it.

title: Twenty Umbrellas by the Gate
paragraphs: At 4:40 on the afternoon of 22 May, rain began ten minutes before the school bell. Sixty students stood at the gate of a middle school in Haizhu without umbrellas. A teacher brought out a plastic box with twenty folded umbrellas inside.

The box was the idea of Ms Zhou, who works in the school office. Anyone can take an umbrella and write a class and a time on a small board. Most come back the next morning. In the first month, seventeen of the twenty returned on time.

The other three caused trouble. One was kept for three days, one was left on a bus, and one was never seen again. Ms Zhou put a note on the box asking students to bring them back. Two umbrellas came back the next day with short notes of apology.
"I did not want a rule with punishment," Ms Zhou said. "A student who forgets is not a thief. After we put the note up, the number of missing umbrellas went from about five a month to one."

The umbrellas cost 30 yuan each, so the first twenty cost 600 yuan, paid from a small fund for student things. By June the school had bought twelve more, and two broken ones had been repaired for 15 yuan each.
The box now stands by the gate all year, not only in the rainy months. On a hot day in September, a student used an umbrella for shade and brought it back the same afternoon.

title: Water Every Other Day
paragraphs: In November, the reservoir above a village in Conghua fell to thirty-one percent of its usual level. The village committee called a meeting and told four hundred people one thing: from 20 November, water would come every other day, for three hours in the morning and three in the evening.

The schedule was printed on three hundred sheets of paper and put on doors and walls. Mr Li, who looks after the pipes, walked the whole line, one and a half kilometers, and found forty leaks. Some were as thin as a finger, but they ran all day.

Not everyone accepted the plan. Families with small children asked for water every day, and a noodle shop said it needed forty buckets a day to stay open. At the meeting, thirty-one people voted for the schedule and twelve voted against it.

"I have two children and a mother who cannot carry water," one woman said. "Every other day is fine for washing. It is not fine for a baby." The committee agreed to keep one tap open all day near the clinic.

New pipe for the worst part cost 8,000 yuan. Sixty families gave 100 yuan each, and the village paid the rest. On 27 November, twelve millimeters of rain fell, and the reservoir rose to thirty-four percent.
The schedule continues until the spring rains. Mr Li checks the tap near the clinic every morning at seven and writes the day of the month on the wall in chalk, so that nobody has to guess.

title: Twenty Minutes of Hail
paragraphs: At 3:15 on the afternoon of 3 April, hail fell on a market in Huadu for twenty minutes. The first stones were the size of peanuts. Then they grew, and some were as large as small eggs. Sellers ran to pull plastic sheets over their vegetables.

The market has sixty stalls under one long roof. Fourteen of the stalls have their own thin covers, and eight of those were torn in the first five minutes. Water came through and ran along the floor between the tables.

About two hundred kilograms of vegetables were wet and had to be sold cheap or thrown away. A seller, Ms Deng, stood on a table and held the corner of a sheet with both hands for ten minutes while her husband tied the other side.

"The ice came down like rice from a bag," she said. "We heard it before we saw it. My first thought was the roof, not the vegetables. A roof costs more than a day of selling, and a day of selling can be made up."

Repairs to the market roof cost 3,000 yuan, and the market closed for one day. Insurance paid 800 yuan. The manager ordered a thicker cover, eight millimeters instead of four, for the fourteen stalls that had lost theirs.
Children from the street collected hail in bowls and put it in a freezer. On the hottest day of July, one family took out a small bag and dropped it into a glass of water.

title: Counting Egrets on the Sand Island
paragraphs: On 8 November, sixteen students from a middle school in Panyu began counting egrets on a sand island in the river. The island is eighty meters long and sits four hundred meters from the school gate. Last winter they counted sixty-one birds. This year the first morning gave them one hundred and nine.

The work starts at half past six, before the light is strong. The class is divided into three groups, and each group watches one part of the island for twenty minutes. They write down every bird that lands, every bird that leaves, and every bird that stays on a nest. Two students share one telescope.

"Last year we counted from the road and thought there were about sixty," said Ms Lin, the biology teacher who leads the group. "This year we sat on the bank with a telescope and found birds we had never seen. The number did not grow. Our eyes did."

Not everyone is pleased. A fisherman who keeps his boat near the island, Mr He, said the birds have eaten the young fish in the shallow water. He asked the school to count somewhere else. The students now start after eight, when his boat has gone out.

By the end of November the group had made twelve counts. The highest was one hundred and thirty-one, on a cold day with a low tide. They also found thirty-four nests, the most in five years. The school will put a sign on the bank in March, asking people to keep boats slow.

title: The Swarm on the Roof
paragraphs: On the afternoon of 14 May, a ball of bees the size of a football appeared on the roof of a middle school in Liwan. It hung from a pipe beside the water tanks, and the hum could be heard on the floor below. A worker guessed there were about twenty thousand bees.

The school closed the stairwell and called a beekeeper, Mr Feng, who keeps forty boxes on a farm in Conghua. He arrived at six, after the bees had stopped flying. He wore a white suit, lit a small fire of dry grass, and brushed the bees into a wooden box.

"A swarm is not angry," Mr Feng said. "It has no honey to protect and no young. It is only looking for a dark place. If you stand still, it will fly around you and go on its way. If you hit it, you will remember the day."

One student was stung on the wrist before the box was closed. The school nurse put ice on it, and he went home at lunchtime. Two parents called the office and asked why the bees were not killed. The head teacher said killing a swarm in a school was more dangerous than moving it.

The work took ninety minutes and cost 400 yuan. Mr Feng took the box to his farm, twelve kilometers away, and set it beside a field of lychee trees. He said the bees would make about fifteen kilograms of honey by next spring, and the school is welcome to the first jar.

title: Four Tons of Water Hyacinth
paragraphs: For two weekends in October, about forty volunteers pulled water hyacinth out of a lotus pond in a park in Liwan. The pond is sixty meters long and thirty wide. On the first morning the plants covered almost half of it, and a small boat could not push through.

The volunteers worked in pairs. One held a rope, the other pulled the plants onto the bank with a rake. The plants came up in heavy wet mats, and each mat weighed as much as a bag of rice. By four in the afternoon they had filled one truck.

The park manager, Mr Deng, had wanted to use a machine. He said a small boat with a cutting bar could clear the pond in two days for 30,000 yuan. The volunteers cost nothing but time, and they took four days. In the end he let them try, and then he helped carry the bags.

"It looks like a green carpet from far away," said a grade 8 student, Wu. "Up close it is a wet mattress full of insects. My arms hurt after an hour, and we had cleared only ten meters. I began to understand why the park gave up last year."

They removed about 4.2 tons in total. Three weeks later, rain and warm water brought the plants back across a third of the pond. The park has ordered a machine for next summer, and Mr Deng has asked the school to come again in April, before the plants begin to grow.

title: A Summer With the Lamps Off
paragraphs: From June to August, a village in Conghua turned off thirty-eight street lamps along a stream between eleven at night and five in the morning. The village wanted to see if fireflies would return. On 20 July, a count along six hundred meters of the bank found about three hundred.

The count was done by eight students and two teachers from a middle school in the town. They walked the bank with small red lights, because white light makes fireflies stop flashing. Each pair counted a section of one hundred meters and wrote the number on a card.

In the summer of 2023, the same walk had found forty-one fireflies. The stream was cleared of rubbish in 2022, but the lamps stayed on all night. A teacher, Mr Xie, said the light was the problem, not the water. The village agreed to try one summer without it.

Not everyone liked the dark. An old woman fell on the road in July and cut her hand, and her son asked the village to turn the lamps back on. The village then kept every fourth lamp on and painted a white mark on the steps near the bridge.

"I walk that road every night," said Ms He, who sells vegetables at the morning market. "At first I carried a torch. Now I know where the stones are. The fireflies stay in the grass beside the water, not on the road, so we can have both." The village will decide in May.

title: Eleven Photos of a Leopard Cat
paragraphs: In March, a forest park in Huangpu put two cameras on trees along a narrow path. The park wanted to know which animals used the path at night. For five months the cameras took 1,900 photos. Most showed leaves moving, rain, and one man walking a small dog.

The cameras were tied at the height of a man's knee and set to take three photos when something warm passed. A worker changed the batteries and the memory card every three weeks, on foot, a walk of about four kilometers. Twice a wild pig knocked a camera out of place.

On 2 August, the eleventh photo of the night showed a leopard cat. It was thin, with a long tail and dark spots, and it looked straight at the lens. Eleven photos followed in nine minutes. The park sent them to a university and waited three weeks for an answer.

"We had reports from farmers for years, but a report is not a photo," said Mr Tan, who manages the park. "Now we know the time, the place, and the size of the animal. We also know it walks alone, which is normal for this cat."

One camera was stolen in June, and the park has not replaced it. Six more will go up in January, on paths where farmers have seen tracks. The park has also asked visitors to keep dogs on a lead after six in the evening.

title: Four Hundred Stickers on the Glass
paragraphs: In September, students at a middle school in Zengcheng began counting dead birds under a glass corridor. The corridor is forty meters long and stands between two buildings. In five weeks they found twenty-three birds, most of them small and brown, lying on the ground in the early morning.

A biology teacher, Ms Zhong, explained the problem. The glass reflected the trees behind it, so birds flew toward a forest that was not there. The class measured the windows and found that the worst ones faced south, toward the trees along the playground.

The class bought four hundred round stickers for 260 yuan and put them on the glass in a grid, twenty centimeters apart. The work took three afternoons. Two teachers said the corridor now looked like a wall of dots, and one asked if they could be removed before a school event.

The next five weeks were better. The students found three birds, down from twenty-three. Two of the three hit the same window, near a door where the stickers had come off in the rain. The class added a second row there and checked the glass after every storm.

"A sticker costs less than a bird," said a grade 8 student, Luo. "But you have to put them in the right place. We put our first ten too high, where birds do not fly. We moved them down a week later, and the number fell." The school has ordered stickers for two more walls.

title: Thirty Caterpillars and a Line of Ants
paragraphs: In April, a grade 7 class in Yuexiu raised thirty caterpillars in a box on the windowsill. The box was made of net and card and stood beside a pot of the plant the caterpillars eat. After two nights, twenty-two of them were gone.

The class found the reason on the third morning. A line of ants was climbing the table leg and passing through a gap in the net, no wider than a pin. The ants took the small caterpillars and left the leaves. A student, Xiao, said the line looked like a road on a map.

They fixed it in two steps. First they put the box on a plate of water, so the ants had to swim. Then they tied the net with a string and moved the table away from the wall. The eight caterpillars that were left grew heavy and stopped eating.

"I thought raising butterflies was about the butterflies," Xiao said. "It is about ants, water, light, and the temperature of the room. For three weeks we did not talk about butterflies at all. We talked about the things that eat them."

Eleven butterflies came out of the box, the last on 28 May. The class let them go in the school garden at lunchtime, and two flew straight into a tree. The ants are still on the table leg. Next year the class will raise silkworms in a box with a water moat from day one.

title: Nine Hundred Seedlings in the Mud
paragraphs: On the morning of 12 April, one hundred and twenty students planted nine hundred mangrove seedlings on a mudflat in Nansha. The flat is exposed for about four hours at low tide, and the work had to be finished before the water came back at half past eleven.

The seedlings came in paper pots, each about twenty centimeters tall. Students dug a hole with a piece of bamboo, put the pot in, and pressed the mud around it with both hands. A worker from the wetland office showed them how deep to go: to the first leaf, no deeper.

The tide came early that day, at eleven. It covered the flat in twenty minutes and took about six hundred seedlings with it. The students stood on the road and watched the small green shoots float away in lines, like a slow parade.

In June they tried again, with a change. Each seedling went in beside a bamboo stick pushed deep into the mud, and a rope tied the plant to the stick. The sticks cost 1,200 yuan, paid by a local company. This time the water took about ninety.

"The first planting was a lesson, not a loss," said Ms Yu, who runs the wetland office. "Mud is not soil. It moves. You cannot plant in mud the way you plant in a garden." A count in October found 710 of the 900 alive, and a third planting is planned for spring.

title: The Snake Under the Black Plastic
paragraphs: On 9 October, a worker found a snake in the vegetable garden of a middle school in Baiyun. It lay under a sheet of black plastic near the tomato rows. The worker, Mr Kuang, called two teachers and kept the garden gate closed.

The snake was about 1.6 meters long, dark brown, with a pale line along its side. A biology teacher, Mr Lei, looked at it from a meter away and said it was a rat snake and not dangerous. Mr Kuang wanted to kill it with a spade. Mr Lei said no.

Getting it into a bag took ten minutes. Mr Lei used a long stick and a rice sack, and the snake struck twice at the stick. Then he drove it three kilometers to a wooded hill and let it go beside a wall of rocks.

The garden had a reason for the snake. For two months, mice had eaten the beans and the young corn, and traps had caught only four. Mr Lei said one rat snake can eat a mouse every few days. Mr Kuang said he did not care and would rather have mice than a snake.

The school spent 800 yuan on a fence of fine net, sixty centimeters high, around the garden. It keeps out snakes and also keeps out frogs, which the students liked. In November the class found three mice in the traps, down from twenty-two in September, and no more beans were lost.

title: The Fish That Did Not Belong
paragraphs: On 18 October, workers drained a pond at a middle school in Tianhe to remove its fish. The pond is twenty-five meters long and held about 300 tons of water. By noon the bottom was mud, and students stood on the bank counting fish in buckets.

The fish were tilapia, a kind that breeds fast and eats the eggs of other fish. Someone had put a few into the pond years ago, probably from a home tank. Last year the school found almost no small shrimp and very few water plants, only tilapia.

The catch came to about 340 fish and sixty kilograms. The school gave forty kilograms to a farm that raises pigs, and the rest went into a deep pit with lime. A few students asked why the fish could not go into the river. A teacher said that was how the problem started.

"One bucket of fish looks like nothing," said Mr Qiu, the science teacher. "But this pond is small and closed. In a river, those same fish swim for years and eat everything. We are not punishing them. We are keeping them where they are."

Refilling took two days. In November the class put in twelve pots of lotus and fifty small native fish from a fish farm in Huadu. The water is still not clear. Mr Qiu says it will take a year, and the sign by the pond now says one thing: no fish, no turtles, no pets.

title: The Book Hospital Outside the Library
paragraphs: In October, twelve students at a middle school in Yuexiu put two tables outside the library and opened a small book hospital. In three weeks they collected 340 damaged books from classrooms, corridors, and the lost box by the gate.

The group sorted every book into three boxes: loose pages, torn covers, and water damage. Loose pages were the easiest and took about six minutes each. Wet books went to a table by the window, where they waited four days under a fan. Of the 340, thirty-eight were too far gone.

The librarian, Ms Deng, asked them to keep one book that a child had drawn on in 2019. "A clean book is not always a loved book," she said. "That one has a cat on page twelve, and the cat is the reason three children read it."

Materials cost 480 yuan: three bottles of glue, four rolls of cloth tape, and a box of paper corners. A history teacher said the money should buy new books. The head teacher answered that 300 new books would cost more than 9,000 yuan, and the library gets 120 yuan a month.

By December, 302 books had gone back on the shelf, and six fell apart again within a week. The hospital meets on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons for fifty minutes. The table by the window is still there, and the fan still runs, even in winter.

title: A Book Cart in the Wet Market
paragraphs: Every Tuesday and Friday morning, Mr Mai, a retired teacher of 68, pushes a cart of books into a wet market in Liwan. He arrives at seven, parks beside the vegetable stalls, and stays for two hours. The cart holds about 120 books, most of them for children.

He built the cart from an old shopping trolley and two wooden boxes. The boxes cost 90 yuan, and a friend painted them blue. In the first month, fourteen books disappeared. Mr Mai did not ask anyone to pay. He wrote a number on the back of every book with a pen.

A fish seller, Ms Tan, complained that the cart blocked the path to her ice box. The market manager measured the space and found 40 centimeters to spare. Mr Mai now parks with one wheel against the wall, and Ms Tan brings him a chair on cold mornings.

"My father sold fish here for thirty years," Mr Mai said. "I taught Chinese for thirty-four years, and I never once saw a child read in this market. Now nine or ten come before school, and they sit on a crate and read while their parents work."

In eight months, he has lost 31 books and gained about 60 regular readers. Two of them now bring books back without being asked. The cart has no rules and no card, only a note on the side: take one, and bring it back when you can.

title: The Shelf by the Canteen Door
paragraphs: In September, a middle school in Tianhe put a wooden shelf by the canteen door and filled it with 180 books. The rule was simple: leave one, take one. By the middle of October, only thirty books were left, and almost nobody had left anything.

A grade 7 class took over the shelf in November. They made a notebook with two columns, one for the book and one for the reader, and wrote a card for each book in their own words. One card said: slow for thirty pages, then very good.

The cards were the change. Students who had never borrowed a book began to read them at lunch, standing up. A boy in grade 8 said he chose a book because the card said the main character was bad at football, like him. He read it twice in one week and told two friends.

Not everyone liked the notebook. A teacher said it made reading into homework, and two students stopped using the shelf for a month. The class kept it anyway, because the number of books that came back rose from eleven a week to forty.

By December the shelf held 210 books, more than it started with, and the cards filled 46 pages. The class now checks the shelf on Friday afternoons. Three books left in September are still missing, and nobody has written a card for them.

title: Twelve Years Late
paragraphs: In April, a small library in Haizhu received a brown paper parcel with no name on it. Inside was a book borrowed in 2012, a bus ticket from 2013, and 20 yuan in paper money. A note said: I am sorry. I moved four times and found this last week.

The librarian, Ms Cen, checked the record. The book had been borrowed on 3 March 2012 by a girl of twelve, and the library had written it off in 2015. Fines stopped in 2021, so nobody owed anything. The parcel had cost 12 yuan to send.

The book could not go back on the shelf. Water had reached the first forty pages, and the cover had come away from the spine. Ms Cen put it in a glass case near the door, with the note and the bus ticket beside it, and wrote one line on a card.

"People think we are angry about late books," Ms Cen said. "We are not. A book that comes back after twelve years tells us something a new book cannot. Somebody kept it through four moves, and then decided it belonged here." She has read the note four times since April.

Six other letters are in the drawer under the desk, all from people who returned books late. Ms Cen reads one on quiet afternoons. In May, the girl, now twenty-four, came to the library and borrowed two books on the same card.

title: Twenty Minutes on a Small Stage
paragraphs: For three weeks in November, twenty-six students at a middle school in Panyu turned a book into a play. They met at lunchtime, from 12:40 to 1:10, in an empty classroom. The book is a story about a girl who looks after a lighthouse for one winter.

The first plan was too long. A full reading of the book took two hours, so the class cut it to twenty minutes and kept four scenes: the boat, the storm, the lamp, and the letter. The boat scene took the longest to build. Two students with no lines made wind with a metal sheet.

The class argued about the ending for a week. The book ends with the girl leaving the island. Half the class wanted her to stay. In the end they voted 17 to 9 for an open ending, in which she stands at the door with a bag and does not move.
"I wanted the sad ending," said Mr Qu, their Chinese teacher. "The students said the sad ending was easy and the open one was honest. They were right, and I did not say so until after the show."

The play was performed twice on 28 November in front of about 200 students. One actor forgot four lines, and a girl in the front row whispered two of them to him. The cloth and paint cost 350 yuan. The lighthouse was a chair with a lamp on it.

title: Forty-One Hours of a Voice
paragraphs: In September, seven students at a middle school in Zengcheng began recording a book for a classmate who cannot see. The book has 180 pages. They worked in a small room beside the music hall, two afternoons a week, and finished the last chapter in November.

The work was slower than they expected. A page took about four minutes to read well, and every mistake meant starting the page again. The group recorded 41 hours in total for a book that takes about nine hours to read aloud. The longest chapter took three afternoons.

They bought one microphone for 260 yuan and shared it. In October the first recorder stopped working, and a teacher lent them another for two weeks. Six chapters were recorded again because a fan in the room could be heard under the voice.

"I asked them to keep the sound of the page turning," the classmate said. "I cannot see where a page ends, but I can hear it, and then I know the story is moving. Nobody had to explain that to them. They just did it."

The book is now on a memory card, with a copy on a school computer. Two of the seven want to record a second book in spring, but the room is used for trumpet practice, so they are looking for a quieter place and a second microphone.

title: The Reading Corner Under the Stairs
paragraphs: In September, a middle school in Baiyun cleaned out the space under the stairs by the gym and put a small reading corner there. The space is three meters long and two wide. It has a shelf, two flat cushions, and one lamp that a teacher brought from home.

The first rain showed a problem. A pipe above the shelf dripped for two days, and nine books were too wet to open. A caretaker had also been storing mops in the corner for years, and he put them back twice in the first week.

The school spent 1,100 yuan on a new shelf and a lamp that fixes to the wall. A worker moved the shelf forty centimeters to the right, away from the pipe, and put a plastic sheet above it. The mops went to a cupboard near the gate. The work took one Saturday morning.

"We thought nobody would come," said Ms Qiu, who looks after the corner. "In the first week, thirty students came in one day, and the space holds eight. We now use a card with a twenty-minute limit, and most students keep to it."

The corner has 24 books, and eleven of them were brought by students. On cold days it is the warmest place in the building, because the pipe runs behind the wall. Ms Qiu says the pipe that ruined nine books now keeps the readers there.

title: Seven Hundred Books on the Playground
paragraphs: On the last Friday of October, a middle school in Huadu held a second-hand book sale on the playground. Families sent in 700 books in two weeks, and forty students sorted them into boxes on the Thursday afternoon. The sale ran from three to six.

The prices were written on colored paper: two yuan for a thin book, five for most, and ten for anything with pictures. A grade 7 student sold 34 books in an hour. By five o'clock, 620 books had gone, and the money box held 3,140 yuan. Two students counted the money twice.

One argument lasted twenty minutes. A parent had given away an art book from 1987 with large pictures of buildings. It was marked at five yuan and sold in the first ten minutes. The parent came back at four and asked for it.

"I did not know what it was worth," the parent, Mr Zhuo, said. "I gave it away because it was heavy. When I saw it go for five yuan, I felt stupid, not cheated." The student found the buyer, explained, and gave back the five yuan.

Mr Zhuo then gave the book back to the school and asked them to keep it in the reading room. The 80 books that did not sell went to a village school in Conghua. With the money, the school bought 120 new books, all chosen by students.

title: Six Hours in a Chair
paragraphs: On 16 November, ninety-two students at a middle school in Huangpu read for six hours in the school hall. They started at nine and stopped at three, with two short breaks. Each student had found sponsors who agreed to pay one yuan for every ten minutes of reading.

The rules were simple. A book had to be a book, not a phone. Students wrote the start and end time on a card, and a teacher signed it. Picture books counted for half. Eleven students fell asleep in the afternoon, and six read picture books all day.

The money came in slowly. Some sponsors paid in cash on the day, but others said they would pay later, and three families never paid. The final count was 2,760 yuan, a little less than the 3,000 yuan the school had hoped for.

"I read 190 pages and then I could not see the words any more," said a grade 7 student, Yan. "The fourth hour was the hardest. My eyes were tired, but my hands were fine, and that is when I understood that reading all day is real work."

The school bought 138 books at about twenty yuan each. They are on a new shelf in the hall, with a card inside each one that says which students read for six hours to pay for it. The shelf was full in December, and four books were out on loan.

title: The Dictionary Without A and B
paragraphs: In September, a village school in Conghua received twelve boxes of donated books, about 300 in all. They were stored in a room beside the office for four days. On the fifth day, heavy rain came through a window that had been left open, and water ran across the floor.

Sixty-one books were wet, and twenty-three of those grew mold within a week. Teachers and students spread the wet books on tables and put two fans in front of them. They changed the paper towels under the pages four times a day for six days.

In the end, 240 books went on the shelves. Sixty more were cut up and made into 500 word cards for the grade 1 and grade 2 classes. A dictionary from 1979 lost its first thirty pages, which held every word beginning with A and B.

"The person who sent the books asked if we wanted to throw the wet ones away," said Ms Liao, the teacher in charge. "We said no. A book with no first pages is still useful if you cut it into cards. Nothing in this room is only rubbish."

The window now has a lock, and the boxes are kept on a wooden platform twenty centimeters above the floor. The 500 cards are in a tin by the door of the grade 2 classroom. The dictionary, without A and B, is on the teacher's desk.

title: A Footbridge Where the Stones Used to Be
paragraphs: For thirty years, people in a town south of the city crossed the canal on eleven flat stones. On March 12, a steel footbridge opened beside the stones, and the old path was closed with a low fence.

The bridge is sixty-eight metres long and three metres wide. It cost 2.4 million yuan, and the town waited five months longer than planned. Workers found two old water pipes under the canal bed, and the pipes had to be moved before the first steel leg could go in.

Not everyone was pleased. The stones were free, and some older residents used them every morning. Mr Tan, who has fished from the bank since 1994, said: "The stones were not safe in the rain, I know that. But I walked on them for thirty years, and I never fell."

The town added a wooden bench at each end and a light that turns on at seven. On the first Saturday, 340 people crossed the bridge, and 62 of them were over seventy. A woman carried a basket of eggs across and said the walk now takes her four minutes instead of eleven.

The stones are still there, under the water and out of reach. The town says it will leave them alone. Mr Tan now crosses the bridge twice a day, and he still stops in the middle to look down at the flat grey shapes below.

title: The Market That Moved Three Hundred Metres
paragraphs: On the first day of April, the wet market in a neighbourhood east of the river moved into a new hall 300 metres away. The old market had stood in the same lane since 1987. The new hall has 96 stalls, cold water, and a roof that does not leak.

Only 54 stalls opened in the first week. The rest stayed in the lane, selling from tables under plastic sheets. The rent in the new hall is 1,800 yuan a month, about 600 more than before, and many sellers said they wanted to wait and see.

The new hall opens at five in the morning, an hour earlier than the old market did. Its floor is dry even after a storm. But the bus stop is 240 metres away, and older sellers must carry their goods in by hand.
Ms Ho, who has sold vegetables for 22 years, said: "My customers know where I stand. If I move, some of them will not follow me, and I cannot pay the rent with customers who do not come."

The market office answered with a plan. Sellers who signed a two-year contract paid no rent for the first six weeks. By June, 81 stalls had moved, and the lane was quiet on weekdays but still busy on Sunday mornings.

The old lane will be cleaned and used for parking. Ms Ho moved in May. She says her sales fell by a third in the first month and came back by August. She still keeps a small wooden stool from her old stall under her new table.

title: The Last Run of the Number 7 Bus
paragraphs: At 9:40 on the last night of June, the number 7 bus left the square for the final time. The route had run for 38 years between the town and the railway station, 14 kilometres each way. The bus company said too few people used it.

The last bus carried 47 passengers, more than it had carried on any night that year. Some brought flowers, and one man played a small radio. The driver, Mr Kwok, had driven the route for 19 years. He stopped at every stop even when nobody was waiting.

A woman gave him a paper bag of oranges, and he put it beside his seat. Mr Kwok said: "I know every hole in this road. I know which corner floods and which tree drops fruit on the roof. A new driver will learn it, but it will take him a year."

The company lost about 900,000 yuan on the route last year. A minibus now runs four times a day, but it does not go to the station. It stops at the top of the hill, and passengers must walk down 180 steps to reach the trains. That walk takes eleven minutes.

The town asked for the route to be kept for another year and was refused. In July, 600 people signed a paper asking for a bus that goes to the station. The company said it would study the idea in December. Mr Kwok now drives the number 12.

title: The Bicycle Shop That Closed on a Sunday
paragraphs: On the last Sunday in October, a bicycle shop on a corner in Liwan closed its door for the last time. It had opened in 1993, and the same family had repaired bikes there for 33 years. The sign above the door was painted by hand.

The shop was small, about 18 square metres. It held 200 tools and a wall of spare parts in small wooden boxes. The owner, Mr Sung, 61, said the rent had gone from 900 yuan a month to 7,200 in twelve years.

In its last month, the shop repaired 74 bikes. Most were children's bikes with flat tyres or loose chains. Mr Sung charged 15 yuan for a repair and often took nothing from students. He said he could not raise the price because the people who came were his neighbours.

One girl came back three times with the same puncture, free each time. Mr Sung said: "People do not repair bikes now. They buy a new one for 400 yuan and leave the old one outside. I am not angry about it. I am just tired of paying for a shop that holds broken things."

On the last day, 30 people came to say goodbye, and someone brought a cake. Mr Sung gave his tools to two young men who fix bikes in the park on Sundays. The shop will become a phone repair counter. The hand-painted sign now hangs above his kitchen door.

title: Nine Hundred Trucks of Silt
paragraphs: For 30 years, the pond in a small park north of the market smelled of old water in summer. In March, workers began to remove the mud at the bottom. The job took 74 days and filled 900 trucks.

The pond is only 40 metres across but 2.1 metres deep in mud. The mud was carried to a field outside the town and left to dry. Workers also took out 11 bicycles, 4 shopping carts, and a metal gate that nobody could explain. The oldest thing found was a coin from 1963.

The work cost 1.7 million yuan, paid by the town and a group of shop owners. Not everyone agreed with the plan. A residents' group wanted the two old trees at the south end kept, and the first plan had them removed to make the bank straight.

The town changed the plan after 240 people signed a letter. The trees stayed, and the bank now curves around them. A low stone wall was built along the north side. New water came in from the canal in May, and 300 small fish were put in during June.

A woman who has lived beside the pond since 1988 said: "I stopped opening my window in July. This year I opened it and smelled nothing. I stood there for a while to be sure." The park added six benches, and the town will test the water every month for a year.

title: The Lane With Two Names
paragraphs: In May, a lane in the old part of town got a new name. The town office changed Market Lane to Old Market Lane, because there is now a second Market Lane near the new hall. The vote was 7 to 4.

The change cost 4,800 yuan for 18 new signs, and it took workers two days to fix them. Two sign makers worked from a small truck. The post office printed 2,000 notices for residents. But 63 people signed a paper asking for the old name to stay.

Mr Lau, 72, who has run a tea shop in the lane for 41 years, said: "My address is on 400 paper bags. My customers have written it on their hands. Now the town tells me the lane is called something else, and I must pay to print again."

The town office said the new name was needed for ambulances and delivery drivers. In April, a food delivery rider spent 25 minutes looking for number 14 because two lanes had the same name. The office also offered to reprint the first 100 bags for each shop, and it answered 90 calls that week.

In the end, both sides got part of what they wanted. The signs now say Old Market Lane in large letters and Market Lane in small ones below. Mr Lau has not changed his paper bags. He says people still find him, and that is what a name is for.

title: The Cinema With Sixty-Four Seats
paragraphs: A cinema that closed in 2017 opened again on the first Saturday of September, but it no longer shows films every night. The town bought the building for 3.2 million yuan and turned it into a community hall with 64 seats.

The seats are the same red seats from 1994, cleaned and repaired by 22 volunteers. The screen is new, and the old projector sits in a corner under a cloth. The first event was a night of old photos, and 130 people came, so 66 of them stood at the back.

The repair was not easy. Rain had come through the roof for years, and the ceiling above row four had to be rebuilt. The town was 80,000 yuan short in June, and a local business paid for the sound system instead.

Some residents wanted the building to be a shop, because the town has no large supermarket. A survey in July found that 58 percent wanted a hall, 21 percent wanted a shop, and the rest did not care. The town will decide on the fourth evening in December.

Ms Chan, who sold tickets there as a student in 1996, said: "I stood in the same place on Saturday and my hands remembered the ticket machine. The machine is gone, but the room still sounds the same when people talk." The hall will open four evenings a week.

title: The Crossing That Took Four Years
paragraphs: On March 3, a pedestrian light began working at a junction in the west of the town, four years after residents first asked for one. The junction has two schools, a clinic, and no bridge within 600 metres. About 900 students use it every school day.

The first request went to the town in 2022. It was refused because the road was too narrow for a light and a turning lane. Residents collected 3,100 signatures in 2024. In November 2025, a boy on a bicycle was hit by a car and broke his arm. He now walks with his mother.

The light cost 260,000 yuan, and workers moved a bus stop 40 metres to make room. In the first week, the town counted 2,400 people crossing each day. Most of them are children. The wait for a green light is 48 seconds.

A shop owner on the corner said: "Forty-eight seconds is long when it rains. But I have watched children wait for it, and they wait. Before, they ran." She has counted them from her window. The shop has been in her family for 30 years.

Not everyone is happy. Drivers say the light adds three minutes to their morning trip, and one delivery company wrote a letter of complaint. The town will count traffic again in September. For now the light stays on from six in the morning until eleven at night.

title: The Public Tap on Corner Street
paragraphs: For 40 years, a public tap at the end of Corner Street gave free water to anyone with a bottle. The tap was put there in 1986 by a shop owner who is now 91. On February 9, the water stopped.
A pipe under the road had broken, and the town turned off the tap while it was repaired. The repair was expected to take ten days. It took 47, because workers found a second leak under the pavement.

During that time, 30 families carried water from a tap at the clinic, 200 metres away. Ms Yip, 68, who fills two bottles every morning, said: "I have a tap at home. I come here because I meet people. For seven weeks the corner was empty, and the street felt like a different street."

She brings a small folding chair too. The town first said the tap would not come back, because the water was not tested and the pipe was in the way of a new drain. Ms Yip wrote to the town office twice.
After 180 people signed a letter, the town changed its mind. It put in a new pipe with a filter and a metal button. The work took four days and cost 12,000 yuan. Most of the money went on the filter.

The tap returned on April 2 with a small sign: drinking water, tested monthly. It runs for eight seconds when pressed. Ms Yip says eight seconds is enough for one bottle, and she now brings a second one for a neighbour.
